# How do you increase app retention?

Meta description: How to increase app retention: find where users drop off, fix onboarding, and give people a reason to come back, including other users.

To increase app retention, find the checkpoint where most users drop off, fix what happens right before it, and give users a recurring reason to return. The strongest recurring reasons are progress, relevance and other people.

Retention is measured per install cohort at fixed checkpoints, usually Day 1, Day 7 and Day 30, and each checkpoint has a different cause. Early drop-off points to onboarding: users never reached the moment the app became useful. Drop-off between the first and fourth week points to habit: nothing pulled users back once the novelty faded. Later drop-off points to value: the app solved a one-time need. Teams that improve retention work one checkpoint at a time, change one thing, and compare the next cohort against the last. Social features address the habit problem directly, because a reply, a follow or a group post creates a reason to open the app that the product team did not have to schedule.

## Where do most apps lose their users?

Most apps lose the majority of new users in the first week. The pattern is consistent across categories even though the absolute numbers differ. The first session decides whether a user sees value at all, and the next six days decide whether that value turns into a habit.

| Checkpoint | What drop-off usually means | First thing to fix |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Users never reached the core value | Shorten onboarding to one clear first action |
| Day 7 | No reason to come back after novelty | Add a recurring trigger tied to progress or people |
| Day 30 | The need was one-time or value is thin | Expand the use case or deepen the core loop |

Read your own curve before choosing a lever. A cohort that loses 70% on Day 1 needs a different fix from one that loses users slowly over a month.

## Which levers move retention the most?

Three levers account for most retention gains. The first is onboarding that gets a user to one meaningful outcome in the first session, measured as the share of new users who complete that action. The second is a recurring trigger, such as a weekly summary or a streak, that brings users back without relying on generic push messages. The third is social connection. Apps that add community features see a retention lift of 10-35%, with 10-30% of monthly active users becoming active contributors, according to published social.plus customer data.

Each lever has a cost. Onboarding changes are cheap to test. Recurring triggers need content or data to be worth opening. Social features need enough activity to feel alive, so they work best when they are seeded before launch.

## How do social features compare with push notifications?

Push notifications are one-way and lose effect as users mute them. Social triggers come from other people, so they carry context the user cares about: someone replied, someone joined your group, someone finished the same challenge. A practical rule is to use push to deliver social events rather than as a substitute for them. Teams typically see engagement rates of 20-50% on community features once a group reaches steady activity, which is hard to match with scheduled messages alone.

## How do you know the change is working?

Compare cohorts, not totals. Pick the checkpoint you targeted, run the change for one cohort, and compare its curve to the previous cohort over 4-8 weeks. Track one leading indicator per lever, such as onboarding completion or the share of users who post once in their first week, so you can see movement before the retention number settles.

## FAQs

### What is a good retention rate for an app?

It depends heavily on category, so compare yourself with apps that solve a similar need. Track your own trend by cohort, since improvement over time matters more than a single benchmark.

### How long does it take to improve retention?

Expect to read a reliable signal within 4-8 weeks of shipping a change. That is long enough for a full cohort to pass the Day 30 checkpoint.

### Should I fix onboarding or add features first?

Fix onboarding first if most users leave on Day 1. Add recurring triggers or social features first if users leave between the first and fourth week.

## Conclusion

Start with your cohort curve, pick the single checkpoint where you lose the most users, and change one thing before that point. If the loss sits in the first month, a recurring reason to return, ideally one that involves other users, is the lever most likely to move it.
